sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of an incomplete, crushed skull with displaced postorbital bones and an almost complete lower jaw.
Scattered plates forming the scleral ring and two elements of the hyoid bone are also present, but no soft tissue or keratinous parts survived.
Researchers initially estimated the wingspan at around 2 meters, but a 2023 revision pushed the size to between 3 and 4 meters, reclassifying it as a mid-sized pterosaur.
A unique dentary crest shape was identified in this species, a feature not seen in other pterosaurs.

The genus and species Europejara olcadesorum were named and described in 2012 by Romain Vullo, Jesús Marugán-Lobón, Alexander Kellner, Ángela Buscalioni, Bernard Gómez, Montserrat de la Fuente, and José Moratalla.
The fossil was recovered from the Las Hoyas site in the La Huérguina Formation, a locality discovered in 1985 that yielded over 20,000 fossils by 2023.
The species name refers to the Olcades, a Celtiberian tribe that inhabited the Cuenca region.
Describers assumed that Europejara had a frugivorous lifestyle, and researchers suggest it was frugivorous or granivorous, playing a role in seed dispersal when angiosperms first appeared.

Mark Witton described tapejarids as adaptable, generalist fliers comparable to modern parrots and crows, likely flying in inland areas due to their short wings while long, well-muscled limbs aided in launching and flapping.

Tapejarid beaks were likely covered by a rhamphotheca, with some possibly having pointed projections similar to omnivorous birds like toucans, and bite-force estimations support a diet of fruits, seeds, and resistant plant matter.
Researchers suggested tapejarids might have had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet including seeds, fruits, insects, and small vertebrates, though this lacks direct fossil evidence.

In 2012, Vullo and colleagues classified Europejara as a member of the pterosaur family Tapejaridae, and in 2016, Rubi Vargas Pêgas and colleagues identified it as the sister group to the Brazilian genera Caiuajara, Tapejara, and Tupandactylus.
The genus name combines 'Europa' with the related genus 'Tapejara'.

Europejara lived in Spain during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, 125 to 121 million years ago, indicating that tapejarids were distributed across Gondwana and Laurasia earlier than previously known.

It is debated whether tapejarids originated in Laurasia or Gondwana, with some researchers arguing that the monophyly of Chinese tapejarines does not support a Laurasian origin, and more research is needed to support interpretations regarding the dispersal patterns and origins of tapejarids, including the relationship of Europejara to South American taxa.
Researchers cautioned that more fossils and gut-content analysis are needed to determine if tapejarids co-evolved with angiosperms or merely dispersed them incidentally.
